strengths: Successfully adapts representation-level steering to autoregressive text-to-music models (specifically MusicGen-Large), enabling fine-grained, training-free control over musical attributes.

Introduces necessary and practical domain-specific modifications for continuous audio, such as mean-pooled feature representation, layer pruning strategies (top-K and exponential weighting), and stochastic injection (Bernoulli gating) to balance prompt adherence with audio quality.

Provides a thorough, multi-faceted evaluation including quantitative metrics (FD, MMD, CLAP), external waveform-based music estimators (chromagrams, onset detectors), real-music evaluation on MusicBench, and a human listening test.
Demonstrates creative and robust time-varying steering applications, such as note crossfading and simultaneous multi-attribute steering.
weaknesses: The fundamental RFM steering technique is adapted from existing work, limiting the core theoretical machine learning novelty of the paper.
Due to the reliance on mean-pooled feature extraction, the method discards sequential ordering, resulting in weaker performance on temporally complex concepts like chord progressions and scales.

The steering directions are primarily trained on a synthetic dataset (SYNTHEORY), and the performance drop on real-world music (MusicBench) indicates challenges in generalizability to highly complex, multi-instrument acoustic contexts.
The human user study is relatively small, involving only 12 participants, which limits the statistical strength of the perceptual results.

strengths: Innovative adaptation of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to text-to-music generation, providing an efficient, training-free mechanism for fine-grained control.
Well-motivated audio-specific extensions, including layer pruning/weighting strategies, deterministic/stochastic temporal schedules, and multi-concept joint steering.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation combining machine learning metrics (FD, MMD, CLAP, probe accuracy), signal-processing-based external estimators (chromagrams, chord/tempo tools), real-world data validation (MusicBench), and a user listening test.
Excellent writing quality and clarity, with detailed appendices containing hyperparameters, mathematical formulations, and pseudocode.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is mostly limited to prompt-only conditioning. It would be stronger to compare against other activation-steering baselines or decoding-time intervention methods.

Strong dependency on the synthetic SynTheory dataset for training probes, which limits transferability to complex real-world musical attributes (such as intricate timbral variations, genre mixtures, or instrumentations) as acknowledged in the limitations.

A noticeable trade-off exists between steering strength and audio fidelity (demonstrated by rising FD/MMD and falling CLAP scores at higher control coefficients), which remains a common bottleneck of activation-space interventions.

strengths: Adapting Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to autoregressive text-to-music models (like MusicGen) is an interesting and creative direction for activation steering.

The paper proposes several sensible and practical steering modifications to improve robustness and prevent out-of-distribution degradation, such as layer pruning (top-K and exponential weighting) and stochastic/deterministic temporal schedules.

The evaluation protocol is comprehensive, combining probe-based evaluation, external waveform-level estimators (e.g., chromagrams, Essentia chord classifiers, librosa onsets), and a subjective human listening test.
weaknesses: The paper lacks comparisons against standard activation steering baselines. To demonstrate the necessity and benefit of the more complex RFM approach, the authors should compare MusicRFM against simpler baselines such as steering with a standard Linear Probe direction or Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA).

The actual control performance is extremely weak for most musical concepts beyond simple pitch classes (notes). As shown in Table 2, the probe accuracy for chords, scales, chord progressions, and time signatures is barely above random chance (e.g., chord steering accuracy of ~0.34 vs. 0.25 random chance, scale steering accuracy of ~0.17 vs. 0.14 random chance). This indicates that the proposed mean-pooled RFM approach struggles with any temporally or structurally complex musical concepts.

The subjective listening test details are incomplete. Table 3 presents mean and standard deviation scores (e.g., 73.46 vs. 59.71) but the paper never defines what scoring scale, protocol (e.g., MUSHRA, ACR), or instructions were provided to the 12 participants. This lack of explanation makes the human evaluation hard to interpret and replicate.

The performance of multi-direction steering (Table 6) shows severe trade-offs; when steering multiple attributes, text prompt alignment (CLAP score) degrades significantly (dropping down to 0.133), and distributional metrics (FD/MMD) escalate, indicating a substantial loss in overall generation quality.

strengths: Innovative Application: The paper successfully adapts representation-engineering and concept-steering (specifically Recursive Feature Machines / Average Gradient Outer Product) from text LLMs to autoregressive text-to-music models (MusicGen).

Audio-Specific Methodological Enhancements: The authors correctly identify that naive activation injection degrades audio quality, and they introduce essential and well-motivated mitigations: layer-pruning (Top-K and continuous exponential weighting), time-varying control schedules, and stochastic application (Bernoulli gating).

Dynamic and Multi-Direction Control: The framework elegantly supports complex control setups, such as crossfading between different notes over time and simultaneous multi-attribute steering (e.g., notes + tempos).

Solid Evaluation Suite: The paper provides comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic (SYNTHEORY) and real-music (MUSICBENCH) datasets, utilizing objective audio quality metrics (FD, MMD, CLAP), probe accuracies, and a subjective human listening test.
weaknesses: Self-Evaluation Bias of Probes: The primary metric for checking if a concept is steered successfully (Probe Acc.) relies on probes trained on the same highly synthetic dataset (SYNTHEORY). While the authors acknowledge this limit, evaluating the steered outputs with independent third-party estimators (e.g., pretrained pitch trackers like CREPE, or chord estimation libraries) would provide much stronger, unbiased evidence of musical correctness.

Lack of Detail in the Listening Test: Section 5.3 lacks essential experimental details. It is unclear what rating scale was used (e.g., 1-5 Likert, or 1-100). Furthermore, identifying fine-grained concepts like 'intervals' or 'chord types' is challenging for laypeople; the paper should clarify if the 12 participants had formal musical training.

Severe Degradation in Multi-Direction Control: As shown in Table 5, steering multiple directions simultaneously results in a massive drop in CLAP alignment (down to ~0.13) and a large increase in FD/MMD. This suggests that the model's text-adherence and audio quality degrade significantly when enforcing more than one constraint, representing a notable limitation for complex musical arrangements.

No Comparison to Inference-Time Optimization Baselines: Although the proposed method is optimization-free at inference, comparing its control precision and audio quality against optimization-based text-to-music control methods (e.g., DITTO) would better contextualize its trade-offs.

strengths: Novel application of Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) to text-to-music (TTM) autoregressive models (specifically MusicGen), enabling fine-grained, activation-space control without fine-tuning or costly per-step optimization.

Effective adaptation of steering to the audio/music domain through layer pruning (top-K and exponential weighting) and temporal schedules (deterministic and stochastic gating), which helps resolve the out-of-distribution audio artifacts of naive steering.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation using both synthetic (SYNTHEORY) and real-music (MusicBench) datasets, evaluated via diverse metrics (FD, MMD, CLAP, and probe accuracy).
Includes a user listening test with 12 participants, demonstrating that the proposed optimizations improve perceived musical control while maintaining audio quality and prompt adherence.
Well-structured manuscript with thorough ablation studies and mathematical details provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Lack of comparison against standard activation-steering baselines such as Activation Addition (ActAdd) or Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). It is unclear how much benefit the AGOP-based RFM approach provides over simpler contrastive or mean-difference activation steering vectors.

The steering effect is quite weak for complex, abstract musical concepts (e.g., chords, intervals, scales, time signatures), with absolute probe accuracies often remaining below 0.35 even at high steering coefficients.
Heavy reliance on synthetic data (SYNTHEORY) for training the probes. As acknowledged by the authors, these probes may struggle to generalize to naturalistic, real-world music generation.
The mean-pooling approach for feature extraction discards temporal ordering, limiting the capability of the system to robustly steer sequential musical concepts like scales or chord progressions.

strengths: Adapting Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) via Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP) to activation steering in autoregressive music models (such as MusicGen) is a novel and timely application.

The paper introduces highly practical, training-free heuristics (layer pruning, exponential weighting, stochastic application) that effectively mitigate the audio quality degradation and prompt drift typically caused by activation steering.

The implementation and evaluation of dynamic temporal schedules (e.g., linear rise/decay, sine modulation, and crossfading between notes) are intuitive and well-supported by both quantitative plots and subjective demos.
The manuscript is well-structured, clear, and provides extensive implementation and hyperparameter details in the appendix, making it highly reproducible.
weaknesses: The control accuracy evaluation relies heavily on probes trained on the highly synthetic SYNTHEORY dataset. As the authors note, these probes may fail to generalize to naturalistic audio, making the absolute validation accuracies in Table 2 difficult to interpret as true musical success.

There is a lack of comparison to simpler activation-steering baselines adapted to the music domain, such as standard Activation Addition (ActAdd) or Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). It is unclear whether the complex RFM/AGOP framework provides a significant performance boost over these simpler, training-free steering vector construction methods.

The multi-direction steering experiments (Table 5) demonstrate severe quality degradation. Under dual steering, the CLAP alignment score drops drastically (from 0.33 to ~0.13) and distributional metrics (FD/MMD) worsen significantly, indicating that the current framework is highly destructive when multiple constraints are applied simultaneously.

The human listening test is quite small in scale, featuring only 12 participants evaluating a small selection of clips. A larger and more rigorous subjective study is typically expected to confidently validate audio quality claims in top-tier generative audio papers.

Due to the reliance on mean-pooling of hidden states, the method is fundamentally limited in handling concepts with temporal dependencies, such as scales, time signatures, and chord progressions, as evidenced by the low probe accuracies in Table 2.
